summary.text: Curved spacetime is the model in which, in Einstein's general relativity, gravity arises from geometry rather than being a fundamental force.
Objects follow geodesics, paths set by the local geometry of spacetime, instead of being pulled directly by distant bodies.
Two principles underlie it: physical laws do not depend on the coordinate system, and gravity's effects match acceleration in small enough regions.

items.prompt: A satellite circles Earth. How does general relativity explain its path?

options.label: Earth, Moon and Sun tug it along a loop
It rides a rigid Euclidean frame stretching across space
A hidden medium pushes it around
It follows a straight line in its local frame, which is a geodesic

items.explain: Spacetime is locally flat, so the satellite always follows a straight line in its local inertial frame, a geodesic.

items.prompt: Could you discover gravity by watching only a single free-falling pebble?

options.label: No, you must compare two separated particles
Yes, its path alone would reveal the field
Yes, but only near the Earth's surface
No, you would have to touch it directly

items.explain: No evidence of gravitation shows up in one particle's motion; relative accelerations of separated bodies reveal it.

items.prompt: One person sits in a small sealed spaceship far from planets, accelerating steadily. Another sits in a small box resting on Earth. What can their experiments tell them?

options.label: The spaceship rider can detect tides
Only the box on Earth feels a force
Only the spaceship can test the speed of light
Neither can tell which setting they are in

items.explain: If tidal effects are too small to measure, no experiment separates gravity from acceleration.

items.prompt: Newton pictured gravity as a force acting instantly across distance. How does Einstein's picture differ?

options.label: The force travels at light speed
There is no gravitational force, only the structure of spacetime
The force acts only inside the Euclidean frame
Gravity depends on the observer's chosen axes

items.explain: Einstein denied both a background Euclidean frame and any force of gravitation.

items.prompt: A scientist insists her laws of physics hold only in the coordinate system she happens to use. Which principle does that contradict?

options.label: The equivalence of accelerating and resting frames
Coordinate independence
The rigid Euclidean frame
The Pythagorean theorem

items.explain: Coordinate independence says the laws of physics cannot depend on what coordinate system one uses.

items.prompt: A flat sheet is rolled into a cylinder without stretching it. What happens to its intrinsic geometry?

options.label: It becomes spherical
It becomes undefined
It changes, because the sheet now curves in space
It stays the same, while extrinsic curvature changes

items.explain: Rolling or folding without stretching changes extrinsic curvature but leaves intrinsic geometry unchanged.

paragraphs.heading: Gravity as geometry
paragraphs.text: Curved spacetime is the model, from Einstein's general relativity, in which gravity comes out of geometry instead of being a basic force as in Newton's picture. Objects travel along geodesics, the paths set by the local shape of spacetime, rather than being pulled directly by faraway bodies. Einstein denied that any fixed Euclidean backdrop stretches through all of space. In his view there is no force of gravity at all, only the structure of spacetime itself.

paragraphs.heading: Newton's picture
paragraphs.text: Newton imagined motion taking place against a rigid Euclidean frame that filled all space and all time. In that picture, gravity was a mysterious force that acted instantly across a distance, no matter what lay in between.

paragraphs.heading: A satellite's straight path
paragraphs.text: Take a satellite circling Earth. In spacetime terms, its path is not set by distant pulls from Earth, the Moon and the Sun; it responds only to conditions right where it is. Spacetime is flat everywhere if you look at a small enough region, so the satellite is always moving in a straight line within its local inertial frame. That is what it means to follow a geodesic.

paragraphs.heading: Tides reveal curvature
paragraphs.text: Riding along with a single falling particle shows no sign of gravity. To find it, you must compare how two separate bodies accelerate relative to each other. Two particles falling toward Earth show tidal accelerations, because the field is uneven from place to place, so each takes its own path through spacetime. Einstein explained these accelerations without any force, as the curvature of spacetime. Each such effect is local, and many of them added up look like a force of gravity reaching out from Earth.

paragraphs.heading: Two key principles
paragraphs.text: The first principle, coordinate independence, says the laws of physics cannot depend on the coordinate system you choose. It widens special relativity's rule, which covered only observers in non-accelerating frames. That raises a puzzle, because in an accelerating frame you feel forces that seem to reveal your motion in an absolute way. Einstein answered with the equivalence principle: in a small enough region, the effects of gravity match those of acceleration. A person in a small spaceship accelerating at g far from any mass, and a person in a box resting on Earth, could do no experiment to tell which one they are in.

paragraphs.heading: Two kinds of mass
paragraphs.text: The equivalence principle can also be put in terms of mass. Newton's law of gravity uses a gravitational mass, m_g, while his second law of motion uses an inertial mass, mᵢ. Nothing in advance says these two should be equal. The equivalence principle says they are one and the same.

paragraphs.heading: Curvature measured from inside
paragraphs.text: On a flat plane the Pythagorean theorem holds for right triangles, and if distances on a surface follow that theorem, the surface must be a flat plane. On curved surfaces it usually fails in its ordinary form. Intrinsic curvature is curvature you can find purely by measuring within the surface, with no need for a higher dimension. Rolling a flat sheet into a cylinder without stretching changes its extrinsic curvature but leaves its intrinsic geometry alone. General relativity treats spacetime's curvature in this intrinsic way, through measurements inside spacetime such as tidal effects.
